title: Anansi and the pot of wisdom
description: Anansi's hoard of wisdom meets a son's practical insight in a fable about humility and shared knowledge.
sourceTitle: Barker and Sinclair, West African Folk-Tales (1917), II
culturalNote: Abridged English adaptation of the collected Fante tale; not an original-language recording.

scenes.title: Wisdom in a pot
scenes.text: In Fante country, Anansi gathered wisdom into a pot. Offended by his neighbors, he planned to keep it from them.

scenes.title: The difficult climb
scenes.text: He carried the pot against his chest and tried to climb a tall tree. The pot kept getting in his way.

scenes.title: Kweku Tsin's advice
scenes.text: His son Kweku Tsin watched below. Why not carry it on your back, the boy suggested. Anansi stopped climbing.

scenes.title: No one knows everything
scenes.text: If all wisdom was inside his pot, how could his son know better? Anansi dropped the pot, scattering wisdom abroad.

title: Tink-tinkje and the highest flight
description: A tiny bird turns strength into a contest of wit in a southern African animal fable.
sourceTitle: James A. Honey, South-African Folk-Tales (1910), Tink-tinkje
culturalNote: Abridged southern African animal tale; this source does not identify it specifically as Zulu.

scenes.title: The birds assemble
scenes.text: The birds wanted a king. They argued about size, strength, and beauty, before choosing a contest of height.

scenes.title: Under Vulture's wing
scenes.text: Vulture climbed toward the sun. Tiny Tink-tinkje rode unnoticed among his feathers, saving the strength of his own wings.

scenes.title: A voice from above
scenes.text: Whenever Vulture claimed the crown, the little bird flew just above him. His small voice declared that he was higher.

scenes.title: The sleeping guard
scenes.text: Angry birds chased the trickster into a hole. Owl guarded it, but fell asleep, and Tink-tinkje slipped away.

title: How stories became Anansi tales
description: Anansi bargains for the ownership of stories, bringing cunning, invention, and the art of telling into one tale.
sourceTitle: Barker and Sinclair, West African Folk-Tales (1917), I
culturalNote: Condensed adaptation of this collected version; animal names and episodes vary across tellings.

scenes.title: Nyankupon's bargain
scenes.text: Stories belonged to Nyankupon. Anansi asked to name them after himself. First, he must deliver bees, a great snake, and a tiger.

scenes.title: The jar of bees
scenes.text: Anansi argued aloud that the bees could not fill his jar. They flew inside to prove him wrong, and he sealed it.

scenes.title: Measuring the snake
scenes.text: He challenged the snake to match a stick, then bound it in place. Another deception helped him lead away the tiger.

scenes.title: A name for the tales
scenes.text: Nyankupon saw that Anansi had fulfilled the bargain. The old stories could now bear the spider's name.

title: The monkey and the shark
description: A coastal friendship becomes a fable of trust, quick thinking, and the danger beneath a generous invitation.
sourceTitle: Edward Steere, Swahili Tales (1870), opening of The Washerman's Donkey
culturalNote: Abridged Zanzibar Swahili framing tale in English; the threat is described without graphic detail.

scenes.title: Fruit above the sea
scenes.text: A monkey shared fruit from a coastal fig tree with a shark. Their friendship lasted through many visits.

scenes.title: An invitation underwater
scenes.text: The shark offered a journey home on his back. Halfway there, he admitted his ruler wanted the monkey's heart.

scenes.title: A quick answer
scenes.text: The monkey said he had left his heart in the tree. Believing him, the shark turned toward the shore.

scenes.title: Safely among the branches
scenes.text: The monkey climbed to safety and refused another journey. He would not mistake a dangerous invitation for friendship again.

title: The chameleon and the second messenger
description: A recorded Zulu origin narrative follows two messengers whose journeys shape the human understanding of mortality.
sourceTitle: James A. Honey, South-African Folk-Tales (1910), A Zulu Version of the Origin of Death
culturalNote: Retells a historical English rendering of a Zulu origin narrative; not a statement of shared contemporary belief.

scenes.title: The first message
scenes.text: In this recorded Zulu telling, the creator sends Chameleon to tell human beings that they will not die.

scenes.title: Along the road
scenes.text: Chameleon travels slowly, stopping to feed along the way. The hopeful message has still not reached the people.

scenes.title: The faster messenger
scenes.text: A second messenger, called Salamander in this translation, is sent with a different message: human beings must die.

scenes.title: The message that arrived
scenes.text: The faster messenger arrives first. The tale holds mortality and lost possibility within the distance between two journeys.

title: The washerman's donkey
description: A cautionary animal fable about persuasion, repeated mistakes, and the warnings we choose to ignore.
sourceTitle: Edward Steere, Swahili Tales (1870), The Story of the Washerman's Donkey
culturalNote: Abridged cautionary fable; includes animal death without graphic description.

scenes.title: A promise from Hare
scenes.text: In the monkey's tale, Hare persuades a washerman's donkey to visit Lion. An attractive promise conceals an ambush.

scenes.title: The first escape
scenes.text: Lion's first attack fails, and the donkey escapes. Hare returns with reassurance, asking the donkey to believe him again.

scenes.title: The second visit
scenes.text: The donkey returns and does not survive. Later, Hare takes the heart and ears that Lion had reserved for himself.

scenes.title: A dangerous excuse
scenes.text: Hare argues that a creature with judgment would never have returned. The monkey finishes his warning and rejects the shark.

title: Goso and the chain of blame
description: A philosophical fable follows grief through a circular chain of blame, questioning certainty and responsibility.
sourceTitle: Edward Steere, Swahili Tales (1870), Goso the Teacher
culturalNote: Condensed adult adaptation about death, retaliatory violence, and circular blame; historical collection context retained.

scenes.title: Beneath the calabash tree
scenes.text: Goso teaches children beneath a calabash tree. A gazelle dislodges a fruit, which falls and kills the teacher.

scenes.title: The search for a cause
scenes.text: His pupils seek someone to punish. They accuse the south wind, then the wall that stops it, then the rat.

scenes.title: A circle of explanations
scenes.text: Each accused points toward another power: cat, rope, knife, fire, water, ox, and tick. The chain finally returns to gazelle.

scenes.title: The cost of certainty
scenes.text: Unable to redirect the accusation, the gazelle is killed. The circular tale leaves the pupils' certainty beside their continuing loss.

title: Sultan Majnun's date palm
description: The opening episode of a larger Swahili adventure follows a youngest son into a royal vigil, a mysterious bird, and the promise of a journey.
sourceTitle: Edward Steere, Swahili Tales (1870), Sultan Majnun, date-palm episode
culturalNote: Adapted opening episode, not the complete tale; this Zanzibar collection reflects Indian Ocean narrative exchange.

scenes.title: The guarded garden
scenes.text: Sultan Majnun tends a rich garden, yet a mysterious bird repeatedly eats the ripe dates before he can taste them.

scenes.title: The youngest volunteer
scenes.text: His older sons fail at keeping watch. The youngest asks for a turn, though his father doubts he will succeed.

scenes.title: Wings above the palm
scenes.text: The young watcher stays awake and seizes the bird's wing. It carries him high above the garden, urging him to let go.

scenes.title: Returning to the ground
scenes.text: He refuses to release it. The bird brings him safely down, beginning the bargain that carries the longer story onward.
